note: Financial argument analysis (SPEC_V2 §68): real-world-shaped claims whose central flaw the learner must identify. Auto-scored; attempts record as stage 'decision' on the concept the flaw abuses.

arguments.claim: Newsletter: "Our AI-innovation fund has returned 31 percent a year for three years. The AI revolution is only beginning - early subscribers who joined in 2023 have nearly doubled their money. Don't be the last one in."

options.text: The past returns are probably fabricated.
Past short-run returns don't persist, the story is already priced, and 'don't be last in' is a FOMO trigger, not evidence.
AI is not a real technology trend.

arguments.debrief: The numbers can be perfectly real - that is what makes the pitch work. The flaw is inferential: three hot years predict little (lesson 46), the priced-in story can't be your edge (lesson 29), and the urgency line is aimed at the bias, not the analysis.

arguments.claim: Forum post: "Bonds are for losers - stocks always win over the long run. Even 2008 recovered. So there is literally no reason anyone with 10+ years should hold anything but 100 percent stocks."

options.text: Stocks don't actually beat bonds historically.
"Always recovered so far" is not "guaranteed", and the argument ignores whether the holder can behaviourally and financially survive the drawdowns on the way.
10 years is much too long a horizon to plan for.

arguments.debrief: The premise (long-run equity outperformance) is historically true; the leap to 'no reason for bonds' fails twice: past recovery is evidence, not certainty (lesson 19's honest phrasing), and lesson 41's capacity/tolerance caps exist precisely because an abandoned 100/0 loses to a held 60/40.

arguments.claim: Bank adviser: "Our managed fund costs 1.9 percent, but you get professional management. A 1.7 point difference versus an index fund is tiny - who cares about 1.7 percent when markets move that much in a day?"

options.text: Daily volatility and a recurring annual fee are different objects: the fee compounds against you every year with certainty, and 1.7 points over decades is a five-figure difference.
Index funds are risk-free, unlike managed funds.

arguments.debrief: The comparison to daily noise is the trick: noise averages out, fees never do. Lesson 18's arithmetic - a certain, recurring −1.7 percent compounds into a massive gap - and lesson 29 adds that the paid-for outperformance rarely materialises after costs.

arguments.claim: Colleague: "Diversification is for people who don't know what they're doing. Concentrating in the two or three companies you've studied deeply is how the great investors got rich."

options.text: Survivorship: the visible concentrated winners hide the concentrated losers, and forgoing free specific-risk removal needs an information edge lesson 29 says private investors don't have.
No investor has ever succeeded while concentrated.
Studying companies deeply is a waste of time.

arguments.debrief: The famous concentrated successes are a survivorship sample - the equally concentrated failures write no books. Diversification's deletion of specific risk is free (lesson 16); declining it is only rational with a genuine, repeatable edge over the market's price.

arguments.claim: Friend: "Never sell winners - taxes eat 31.4 percent of the gain. I've held a fund I hate for years just to avoid the tax bill."

options.text: Correct - realizing gains is always a mistake.

Tax deferral is a real advantage, but only on the gain - paying 31.4 percent of the profit to escape a fund with a real ongoing flaw (cost, concentration) can be cheap; the tax tail shouldn't wag the portfolio dog.
Taxes on funds don't exist inside a CTO.

arguments.debrief: Deferral genuinely compounds (lesson 49) - the grain of truth. But the tax falls on the gain, not the balance, and holding a structurally bad position to avoid it costs more via lesson 18's recurring drag. Wrappers (lesson 50) and honest arithmetic, not tax phobia, make the call.
